title: Key Bridge rebuild progresses with first piles driven into the Patapsco riverbed
summary: Construction crews are beginning to drive massive cylindrical piles into the Patapsco riverbed, part of the next stage of the expedited rebuilding Baltimore’s fallen Francis Scott Key Bridge.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters November 6, 2025

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters November 6, 2025

Construction crews are beginning to drive massive cylindrical piles into the Patapsco riverbed, part of the next stage of the expedited rebuilding of Baltimore’s fallen Francis Scott Key Bridge.

If everything goes right, some of these steel piles could later form part of the new Key Bridge, engineers said. But mainly, they are test subjects.

Once the piles are positioned deep within the river bottom, crews will top them with a large yellow cap that functions as a hammer, striking the pile repeatedly to test its strength. Eventually, the blows will reach a maximum force of about 10 million pounds, said Brian Wolfe, the director of project development at the Maryland Transportation Authority.

“We know the piles can carry the load, just based on steel being a known material. What’s unknown is that river bottom,” Wolfe said. “This is to verify: How far down do we need to drive those piles into it, in order to get the load that we need to carry the bridge?

During a sampling effort in the Patapsco River, engineers discovered that a substantial upper layer of the riverbed, the first 60 or 70 feet, is “soupy,” Wolfe said. In other words, it is much too soft to support an enormous cable-stayed bridge.

But beneath all of that muck is an “extremely hard” layer, Wolfe said, and the piles will need to burrow deep into that layer in order to hold up the bridge.

Each pile is more than 200 feet long and 8 feet in diameter, and weighs around 340,000 pounds, Wolfe said. So, maneuvering them requires some of the East Coast’s largest cranes, as have several other parts of the complex effort to demolish the old bridge and bring in the new.

Already, six piles have been placed in the Patapsco River, and crews are busy cutting excess, rusty steel from the top of each piece, leaving behind sections that have been coated to prevent water intrusion and degradation, said Jason Stolicny, deputy director of project development at the MdTA. Next, a steel frame will be placed on the piles as they are carefully monitored during testing to see how they withstand the hammer blows.

Still, reminders of the terrifying crash more than a year and a half ago remain on the site, including a large concrete pier, now surrounded by barges, cranes and construction equipment.

On March 26, 2024, a cargo ship bound for Sri Lanka, carrying more than 4,600 shipping containers, struck one of the bridge’s support columns after a mechanical failure on the ship, sending the structure careening into the water, and killing six construction workers who had been working on the roadway above.

Even though work is underway on the new bridge, which has a target completion date of fall 2028, crews are still removing large pieces of the old one. That demolition work is roughly halfway complete, engineers say, and is expected to continue through early 2026.

Currently, crews are focused on removing the remaining bridge spans that run over the land, Stolicny said. That’s because they hope to erect a “temporary access trestle,” Stolicny said, essentially a pedestrian bridge that will allow workers to easily reach the bridge site on the river.

Initial projections placed the cost for the bridge replacement around $1.8 billion, with a 2028 reopening date. But the MdTA’s chief engineer Jim Harkness was less than certain about the completion date Wednesday, saying that his team is still working with its contractors to determine the project schedule and estimate.

But Harkness added that fall 2028 is still the target, and that the authority is moving at “breakneck speed” to get the new bridge built.

An official groundbreaking is likely in the next few months, said Harkness, who noted that the new bridge will have rigid fenders, added with the intent to protect the piers from potential ship strikes.

The authority’s contractor, Kiewit Corp., is about 70% finished designing the new cable-stayed bridge, Harkness said, with an expected completion date at the end of this month. The design work started last September, Harkness said.

“We’re expecting to have 2,000 plan sheets make up the design for this bridge. If you printed all that out, you’d have a stack of paper nearly 8 inches tall,” Harkness said. “Something that would normally take a team years, we’ve been able to accomplish in 14 months.”

One potential hurdle that has cropped up in recent months is the federal government, which pledged in the Biden administration to fully fund a Key Bridge replacement. But President Donald Trump has hinted that his administration may not do that, although state leaders note that the funding agreement was written into law.

In a September letter to state officials, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that “any reliance on race- or sex-conscious factors in contracting decisions could introduce significant legal vulnerabilities and inefficiencies in the management of the project,” an apparent reference to state programs to bolster minority and women-owned businesses in contracting efforts.

Kiewit, the bridge contractor, has committed previously to a goal of using 26% “disadvantaged business enterprises,” including businesses that are at least 51% owned and controlled by one or more minority individuals.

Duffy also said his department hopes to ensure that the project is delivered “on time, on budget, and in compliance with the law.”

“We will continue to work with the Trump Administration to find ways to reduce costs and rebuild faster,” Gov. Wes Moore (D) said in a statement responding to Duffy’s letter. “We anticipate the price estimation process to be finalized in the coming months and we will provide regular updates.”

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

As work continues with the piles, crews will employ a technology called a “bubble curtain” to soften underwater noise from the hammer blows, minimizing impacts to fish and other creatures in the river, officials say. Using air compressors on a barge at the site, crews create Jacuzzi-like bubbles around the piles, capable of dampening sound.

Weeks worth of data from the hammer blows will determine whether the new bridge’s foundation is strong, and construction can proceed apace, Wolfe said. So far, the pile installation has gone as planned, he said, matching the crew’s expectations about the sediment at the bottom of the river.

“It’s essentially confirming what we had anticipated from the boring program,” Wolfe said. “[The piles] went through that soupy material right to that hard layer, like we had anticipated.”
